rudiments:blockdesc-rettingvat:
Legacy block — water retting now uses a sealed barrel; existing vats still work but can no longer be crafted.
Water-rets rippled flax or fresh nettle. Faster than field retting. Quality depends on timing — collect at the brief fine window for the best fibre, or leave it to rot.

Lime retting: right-click the vat with quicklime to load a lime modifier. One unit is consumed when a new retting batch starts. Lime makes retting 2.5× faster but quality is capped at Standard — fine fibre is never produced, and the rot window is tighter. Useful for bulk production when quality is not the priority.

rudiments:itemdesc-scutchsword: A wooden swingle with a deliberately dull edge, so it scrapes the woody boon away without cutting the fibre. Load a scutch board with broken bundles, then hold <hk>leftmouse</hk> against the board to strike.
rudiments:item-handbooktext-scutchsword: Load a scutch board with broken bundles, then hold leftmouse on the board to strike them. The blade rides on the boon, so early strokes cost the fibre nothing. Once an end runs clean the strike sharpens in pitch and pale fluff comes off instead of brown shives — that is the moment to sneak + rightmouse and turn the bundle. Keep beating a clean end and the blade starts cutting the long line into short tow. Costs 1 durability per stroke.
rudiments:scutchboard-empty: Empty. Right-click with broken flax or nettle bundles to load it.
rudiments:scutchboard-wrongquality: That bundle doesn't match the batch already on the board.
rudiments:scutchboard-inprogress: This batch is already part-scutched — collect it before loading more.
rudiments:scutchboard-side-near: Working the near end of the bundle.
rudiments:scutchboard-side-far: Working the far end of the bundle.
rudiments:scutchboard-cleanliness-vague: The bundle is {0} clear of boon.

rudiments:scutchboard-blockhelp-flip: Turn the bundle end for end
rudiments:itemdesc-flaxbundle-unprocesse: Right-click bare ground to place in a stook to cure the stems before rippling. Flax cut in bloom rets to finer fibre but carries no seed; fully mature flax rets coarser and yields seeds and grain when rippled.
rudiments:itemdesc-flaxbundle-cured: Stems are dried and ready for rippling. Ripple on a ripple block to comb out the seed heads (mature bundles yield seeds and grain; bloom-cut bundles yield none), then ret.
rudiments:itemdesc-flaxbundle-rippled: Seal it in a water barrel to ret it (fast) or lay it on the ground (field retting). Retting time decides the fibre quality.
rudiments:itemdesc-flaxbundle-retted: Dry it on a drying rack
rudiments:itemdesc-flaxbundle-broken: Load onto a scutch board and beat it with a scutching sword to knock the woody boon free. Turn the bundle halfway through, and stop once it runs clean — over-beating cuts the long fibre into tow.
rudiments:itemdesc-nettlebundle-unproces: Stings bare hands. Right-click bare ground to stook-cure it before retting.
rudiments:itemdesc-nettlebundle-cured: Cured and ready to ret. Right-click bare ground to field-ret it, or seal it in a water barrel.
rudiments:itemdesc-nettlebundle-retted: Dry it on a drying rack
rudiments:itemdesc-nettlebundle-broken: Load onto a scutch board and beat it with a scutching sword. Nettle carries much more boon than flax, so expect around half again as many strokes per end.
rudiments:itemdesc-coarsefibers: Rough low-quality fibres from poorly-retted material. Suitable only for rope and basic cordage.
rudiments:itemdesc-finefibers: Smooth, strong fibres from well-retted and carefully processed material. Twist into fine cord for durability bonuses on bows and tools.
rudiments:itemdesc-finecord: A tightly-twisted cord of fine fibres. Use in place of flaxtwine in bow and tool recipes for a significant durability increase.
rudiments:itemdesc-nettlerhizome: A root cutting from stinging nettle. Right-click on fertile soil to establish a new wild patch — no farmland needed. Can be cooked on a fire.
rudiments:itemdesc-cookednettlerhizome: Roasted nettle root — earthy and filling.
rudiments:itemdesc-nettlefiber: Strong bast fibre - three make a length of twine
rudiments:itemdesc-nettleleaves: Young nettle leaves. Edible raw but the residual sting causes minor damage — cook them first to remove it completely.
rudiments:itemdesc-linseedoil: Pressed from flax seeds. Edible, and burns as lamp fuel
rudiments:itemdesc-linseedcake: Pressed seed residue - kindling or animal fodder
rudiments:blockdesc-nettlestub: The root crown left after cutting mature nettle. It will regrow on its own — or shovel it up to get a rhizome for transplanting.
rudiments:blockdesc-ripple-*: A tool used for extracting seeds from flax
rudiments:blockdesc-break-*: A tool used for breaking dried flax or nettle
rudiments:blockdesc-hatchel-*: A tool used for extracting fibres from broken flax or nettle
rudiments:blockdesc-dryingrack-*: Dries retted bundles. Warm, sheltered, dry weather works fastest; rain stalls it. Preserves fibre quality.
rudiments:blockdesc-fieldretting-*: Field-rets rippled flax or cured nettle laid flat on the ground. No crafting required — right-click bare ground with bundles. Damp weather advances retting; dry spells stall it (no quality loss). Watch the info text for the brief fine-fibre window.
rudiments:blockdesc-stook: Standing sheaves for curing or drying bundles outdoors. Cures green unprocessed bundles into cured stems (arid weather required). Also dries retted bundles, but rain will reset progress and degrade fibre quality — use a sheltered drying rack for a safe outcome.
rudiments:blockdesc-oilpress: Hold flax seeds against it to press out linseed oil and seed cake
rudiments:blockdesc-scutchboard-*:
An upright notched plank tenoned into a block. The notch holds the bundle and guards the hand holding it. Right-click with broken flax or nettle bundles to load it, then hold leftmouse with a scutching sword to beat the woody boon off.

Only the end facing you is being worked — sneak + rightmouse turns the bundle so you can do the other half. Listen for the strike: while there is boon left it lands dull and throws brown shives, and once that end runs clean it sharpens and throws pale fluff. That is your cue to turn it, because from then on the blade is cutting the long line into short tow.

Right-click empty-handed to collect. A cleaner batch grades higher (never above what retting granted); a beaten one comes off as coarse fibre instead of scutched bundles. Better workmanship in the notch holds more bundles and clears more boon per stroke.
rudiments:blockdesc-mechscutcher:
An axle-driven scutch mill. Feed it dried bundles and it automatically breaks and scutches them into scutched bundles. You still need to hatchel those bundles by hand to extract the final fibre.

Mill scutching is fast but wasteful: the beating arms shred a share of every batch into tow, which drops out at the mill as coarse fibres. Fibre quality is untouched — this costs yield, not grade.
rudiments:item-handbooktext-flaxbundle-u: Step 1 of 7: Right-click bare ground to place the fresh flax in a stook. Arid weather cures the green stems (about 1 in-game day). Rain stalls the process.
rudiments:item-handbooktext-flaxbundle-c: Step 2 of 7: Comb the cured flax by holding rightmouse on a ripple. Mature bundles give up their seeds and grain here; bloom-cut bundles have none to give.
rudiments:item-handbooktext-flaxbundle-r: Step 3 of 7: Ret the rippled flax by sealing it in a barrel of water (fast, controlled) — sealing immediately turns it into an open retting bath — or right-click bare ground to lay it out for field retting (slow, free). Bloom-cut bundles ret to standard fibre with a brief fine window worth catching; mature bundles ret coarse and settle at standard. Everything rots if left too long.
Step 4 of 7: Dry the retted flax. Safe option: a drying rack preserves quality. Risky option: right-click bare ground to stook it outdoors — rain will reset progress and degrade quality.
rudiments:item-handbooktext-flaxbundle-d: Step 5 of 7: Break the dried flax by holding rightmouse on a break.
rudiments:item-handbooktext-flaxbundle-b:
Step 6 of 7: Scutch the broken flax. Right-click a scutch board to load it, then hold leftmouse with a scutching sword to beat the boon off.

Only the end facing you is worked. When the strike sharpens in pitch and pale fluff replaces the brown shives, that end is done — sneak + rightmouse to turn the bundle and do the other half. Keep beating a clean end and the blade starts cutting the long line into short tow, which comes off as coarse fibres instead.

Right-click empty-handed to collect. Cleanliness sets the grade, but never above what retting granted; how much you over-beat sets how much of the batch survives as line.
rudiments:item-handbooktext-flaxbundle-s: Step 7 of 7: Extract flax fibres from the scutched flax by holding rightmouse on a hatchel. Higher fibre quality yields more fibre.
rudiments:item-handbooktext-nettlebundle: Step 1 of 6: Wear gloves — bare-handed handling stings! Right-click bare ground to place in a stook and cure the fresh stems (arid weather, ~1 day). Nettle skips rippling.
Step 2 of 6: Ret the cured nettle by sealing it in a barrel of water (fast) — sealing starts an open retting bath — or right-click bare ground to field-ret it (slow). Timing sets the fibre quality.
Step 3 of 6: Dry on a drying rack (safe, quality preserved) or stook outdoors (risky — rain degrades quality).
Step 4 of 6: Break the dried nettle on a break, then hatchel it for fibres.

Step 5 of 6: Scutch the broken nettle. Load it onto a scutch board, beat it with a scutching sword (hold leftmouse), and sneak + rightmouse to turn it once the near end runs clean. Nettle holds far more boon than flax and needs roughly half again as many strokes per end. Collect empty-handed, then hatchel for fibres.
Step 6 of 6: Hatchel the scutched nettle to extract nettle fibres.
rudiments:item-handbooktext-nettleleaves: Harvested from young nettle plants (stages 3–6). Raw leaves cause minor damage when eaten — the stinging compounds survive into the picked leaf. Cooking them in a pot removes this completely; nettle soup is a worthwhile early-game food. Handling: use the slow careful harvest (hold rightmouse) to pick without being stung, or wear gloves and break normally.
rudiments:item-handbooktext-coarsefibers:
Low-quality fibres produced when retting is too brief or conditions were poor. They lack the strength and smoothness of standard fibres, so they are only suitable for rough rope and cordage — not for fine cloth or bowstrings.

Use: coarse fibres can only be twisted into rope. They will not substitute for standard or fine fibres in twine, cloth, gambeson, or bowstring recipes.
rudiments:item-handbooktext-finefibers: The best-quality bast fibre, produced only by careful retting at the right stage. Twist four of them together into fine cord, which imparts a durability bonus when used in bow or tool crafting.
rudiments:item-handbooktext-finecord: A precisely-twisted cord of fine bast fibres — uniform, strong, and resistant to repeated stress. Replaces flaxtwine in bow recipes for a significant durability bonus (+50/100/150 by tier). Also used in linen gambeson head and leg armor crafting for +200 durability.
rudiments:item-handbooktext-nettlerhizom: A root crown dug from mature stinging nettle (stage 8 or 9). Hold a <hk>shovel</hk> and right-click the plant to carefully extract it — the plant is destroyed. Right-click fertile soil with the rhizome to establish a new patch anywhere without needing farmland. Wild nettle also spreads naturally by rhizome over time.
rudiments:item-handbooktext-nettlefiber: A strong plant bast fibre. Three nettle fibres spin into a length of twine - nettle is stronger than flax, so it needs fewer.
rudiments:item-handbooktext-linseedoil: Pressed from flax seeds on a seed oil press. A nourishing edible oil that also burns as lamp fuel.
rudiments:item-handbooktext-linseedcake: The pressed residue left after extracting linseed oil. Useful as kindling or animal fodder.
rudiments:craftinginfo-flax-text:
Two fibres, one craft
Rudiments turns flax and stinging nettle into usable fibre through a multi-step process.

Flax (7 steps)
Harvest timing matters — and flax drops nothing until it has bloomed. Cut it in bloom (stage 8) for the best fibre: those bundles ret from standard quality with a shot at fine, but carry no seed at all. Let it stand to full maturity (stage 9) and the stems coarsen like nettle — bundles ret from coarse and top out at standard — but the plant now drops seeds, and rippling the bundles yields more seed and grain for linseed oil.
1 - Stook-cure the fresh bundles: right-click bare ground to place a stook. Arid weather cures the green stems in about 1 day. Rain stalls this step.
2 - Ripple the cured bundles on a ripple to comb out the seed heads — mature bundles yield seeds and grain, bloom-cut bundles none.
3 - Ret the rippled flax. Field retting (free): right-click bare ground to lay them out flat. Water retting: fill a barrel with water, add the bundles and seal it — the barrel immediately reopens as a retting bath and the bundles ret faster than in the field. For a quicker lime ret (capped at standard quality, tighter rot window), make limewater first and seal the bundles in that instead. Dry spells stall field retting — no harm, just wait for rain.
4 - Dry the retted flax. Safe: a drying rack preserves quality. Risky: right-click bare ground to stook it outdoors — rain resets progress and degrades quality.
5 - Break the dried flax on a break.
6 - Scutch the broken flax on a scutch board. Right-click the board to load it, hold leftmouse with a scutching sword to beat the boon off, listen for the change — the strike sharpens and pale fluff replaces brown shives when that end is clean — then sneak + rightmouse to turn the bundle and work the other half. Right-click empty-handed to collect.
7 - Hatchel the scutched flax for fibres.

Scutching, under and over
Under-scutching costs you nothing in fibre but leaves boon bound in, and the batch grades down — a bundle that never gets clean comes off coarse no matter how well it was retted. Over-scutching is the opposite trap: once an end is clean the blade has no boon left to ride on and starts cutting the long line into short tow, which you collect as coarse fibres instead of scutched bundles. Neither is a timer; both fall out of the same curve, and the change in the strike tells you where you are on it. Scutching can only lose the quality retting granted, never exceed it. Nettle carries far more boon than flax and wants about half again as many strokes per end.

Nettle (6 steps)
Stinging nettle grows fast but needs careful handling. Young plants (stages 3–6) give edible leaves — hold rightmouse on the plant for a slow careful harvest with no sting; or wear gloves and break normally. Older plants (stages 7–9) yield nettle bundles.
Nettle skips rippling. Right-click bare ground with fresh bundles to stook-cure them first, then right-click again with cured bundles to field-ret, or seal them in a water barrel. Then dry, break, scutch, and hatchel for nettle fibres.

Fibre quality
Harvest timing sets the range, retting timing decides where you land in it. Bloom-cut flax rets straight to standard fibre and may open a brief fine window (the best fibre — more yield at the hatchel and durability bonuses on bows and armour) before settling back to standard. Mature flax and nettle ret to coarse first, improve to standard with time, and can never reach fine. Everything rots if abandoned. Water retting in a barrel is quick; field retting is slow. Watch the block's info text to catch the fine window.

Automation & oil
A mechanical scutch mill driven by an axle automatically breaks and scutches dried bundles into scutched bundles ready for hatcheling — but the mill is a throughput-for-yield trade, exactly as it was historically: the beating arms shred a share of every batch into tow that drops out at the mill as coarse fibres. Quality is untouched, only the yield. Hand scutching keeps more of the line; the mill keeps more of your time. A seed oil press turns mature flax seeds into linseed oil.

rudiments:itemdesc-handcards: A pair of wire-toothed carding brushes for combing washed wool into rolags. Hold washed wool in your off hand and brush it between the cards.
rudiments:item-handbooktext-handcards: Hold washed wool fibers in your off hand and the cards in your active hand, then hold rightmouse to brush the wool into a rolag, ready for twisting into twine. Costs 1 durability per fiber carded.
rudiments:handcards-need-fibers: Hold washed wool fibers in your off hand to card them
rudiments:itemdesc-rolag-*: Washed wool carded into an airy roll, ready to be twisted into twine
rudiments:item-handbooktext-rolag: Made by carding: hold washed wool fibers in your off hand and brush them with hand cards (hold rightmouse). Four rolags twist into wool twine in the grid; a drop spindle or spinning wheel spins two per twine.

game:itemdesc-clay-porcelain: A white, iron-free body of blue clay and silica. Fires white and translucent — but only in a fully sealed kiln. Anything less and it comes out as shards.
rudiments:handbook-ware-text: Fired clay is not one material. Which of the three bodies you are holding decides whether it holds water, how the food inside it keeps, and how easily it breaks. Earthenware is what unmarked fired clay is, and what every pit kiln produces. It is fired below the point at which the body vitrifies, so it stays porous — above 3% water absorption — and it genuinely weeps. A jug of water left standing will be a jug of nothing by morning. See Water and porous ware. Stoneware is the same clay taken hotter, in a beehive kiln, until the body glasses over. At or below 3% absorption it stops sweating altogether. Anything that comes out of a beehive kiln is stoneware — you do not need different clay for it, only a better kiln. Porcelain is not a firing technique at all. It is a different body, made from a different clay, and it goes below 0.5% absorption. It also carries a real advantage for stored food. See Porcelain. That is why sealing is a property of the tier rather than a separate mechanic: a vitrified pot has no pores left for water to travel through. A glaze achieves the same thing by putting a layer of glass over a body that never vitrified. The trade is that the finer the body, the more brittle it is. See Handling pottery.
rudiments:handbook-handling-text: Pottery breaks. Two ways. Wear. Every time you actually use a vessel — drink from it, fill it, empty it, pour from it — there is a small chance it fails in your hands. Earthenware 0.1%, stoneware 0.5%, porcelain 1.5%. In practice that is a median of roughly 693, 138 and 46 uses. Wear is texture, not a tax; you will lose the occasional bowl and that is the point. Yes, porcelain is the most fragile, and that is not backwards. Porcelain's flexural strength is genuinely higher than earthenware's — it is a stronger material by that measure. But it is thin-walled and brittle, and it shatters where thick porous earthenware merely chips. The finest ware is the ware you handle most carefully. Dropping. Throw a fired pot on the floor and it shatters, leaving shards. So does one that falls far enough to land hard. Anything inside it spills out rather than being destroyed with it. Three things are exempt. Pottery scattered when you die survives — your corpse run is punishment enough. Unfired clay deforms rather than shattering, so greenware is safe. And bricks, tiles, shingles and kiln parts are building material, not vessels; they are exempt whether they are in item or block form. The practical consequence is that moving a lot of pottery by hand is now genuinely risky. Ground storage and crates are the right answer, and they always were.
rudiments:handbook-water-text: An unglazed earthenware vessel leaks. Not quickly enough to see, but a full one is half empty in six hours and dry in twelve. The rate is a share of that vessel's own capacity, so a 1-litre bowl and a 3-litre jug both empty on the same clock — the jug does not last three times as long for being bigger. Sealed means stoneware, porcelain, or any glaze. A sealed vessel holds its contents indefinitely. Nothing else does. This is not an invented inconvenience. It is why the potter's ladder exists at all: an earthenware jug that weeps is the problem that vitrification and glaze were both invented to solve. On the watering can. The spouted, rosed watering can is a late invention — roughly 17th century onward in Europe. Before it, gardeners used thumb-pots and chantepleures, and ollas — buried unglazed jars that seep on purpose — predate both by millennia. Vanilla handing you one on day one is the ahistorical part. Putting it behind a sealed body is a correction, not a nerf.
rudiments:handbook-porcelain-text: Porcelain is not a firing technique applied to ordinary clay. It is a body: kaolin plus petuntse, fired to around 1300–1400 °C. Europe had kilns hot enough for centuries and still could not make porcelain, because it did not have the clay. Kaolin runs about 39–40% alumina and 46–48% silica and is essentially iron-free, which is the entire point — it fires white and translucent. Fire clay runs 25–35% alumina and carries meaningful iron oxide and alkali fluxes, so it fires buff or brown and speckles. Kaolins do qualify as super-duty fire clays, so the implication runs one way only: kaolin is a fire clay; a fire clay is not kaolin. Two routes to porcelain clay, both from blue clay. Red clay will not do. 1 — Quartz. Crushed quartz plus blue clay. Quartz comes from a pulverizer, which means bronze-tier pounders and mechanical power. Calcined flint and crushed quartz are the same oxide doing the same job — flint is cryptocrystalline quartz — and what separates fire clay from porcelain clay is therefore the clay, not the silica. Blue clay plus silica is a white body; red clay plus silica is a buff one. Staffordshire adopted flint from about 1720 and converted water-powered corn mills into flint mills to keep up with demand. 2 — Bone china. Powdered flint and bonemeal with blue clay. No metal at all: a firepit and a quern will do it. This is the historical answer to exactly the problem you have. English potters could not source petuntse, so from Spode's work in 1789–1793 they substituted bone ash; the standard formula settled at 50% bone ash, 25% china clay, 25% Cornish stone, fired around 1250 °C. It yields less porcelain clay per unit of blue clay than the quartz route. One admission: crushed quartz stands in for petuntse, and petuntse is really a feldspathic rock that fluxes as well as supplying silica. There is no feldspar in this world. Route 2 is not a deviation at all. Firing it is the hard part. Porcelain greenware needs an even, fully sealed soak. In a beehive kiln with every door shut it comes out white. With any door ajar, or in a pit kiln, it comes out as shards. Molds and crucibles are not made from it — they are fire clay for the heat, and you want the iron there. What it buys you. Below 0.5% water absorption means almost no exchange with what is inside. Food in a porcelain storage vessel keeps markedly longer than in any other ceramic — the vessel's own tooltip will tell you by how much.
rudiments:handbook-kilns-text: The pit kiln is where everyone starts, and it makes earthenware and nothing else. It cannot get hot enough or even enough to vitrify a body. The beehive kiln vitrifies. Everything that comes out of one is now stoneware — sealed, no longer porous, and slightly more brittle for it. The colours it gives you are unchanged: the same four door counts give the same four results they always did. It is a downdraft kiln, and that is the whole reason it exists. Flame rises, deflects off the dome and is pulled back down through the ware to flues in the floor. That even heat is why downdraft displaced updraft everywhere it could afford to. The door rule is the same argument in miniature — a door left ajar spoils an otherwise even firing, which is why porcelain demands all of them shut. (The game's convention is that more open doors darkens the ware. Real oxidation lightens it. That is vanilla's convention and this mod rides it rather than contradicting it.)
rudiments:handbook-fireclay-title: Why this is not porcelain clay
rudiments:handbook-fireclay-text: Fire clay is chosen for heat, and you tolerate its iron. Porcelain clay is chosen because the iron is not there. Fire clay runs 25–35% alumina with meaningful iron oxide and alkali fluxes, so it fires buff or brown and speckles; a porcelain body is essentially iron-free and fires white and translucent. Kaolins do qualify as super-duty fire clays, so the implication runs one way only — kaolin is a fire clay, but a fire clay is not kaolin. Molds and crucibles stay fire clay for exactly the reason porcelain would be wrong in them. See Porcelain.
